query: If the ticket types that create the heaviest agent workload were reduced, how much would resolution time drop?

per_column.name: ticket_type_primary
per_column.rationale: The query explicitly targets 'ticket types that create the heaviest agent workload' as the lever to reduce. This is the intervention variable and is directly named.

per_column.name: agent_assignment
per_column.rationale: Which agent handles a ticket can influence both the ticket type routed to them (specialization) and the resolution time (agent skill/speed), making it a common cause. Not named in the query.

per_column.name: ticket_scope_extent
per_column.rationale: Scope (single user vs enterprise-wide) plausibly affects both the ticket type distribution and resolution time, acting as a common cause. Not named in the query.

per_column.name: ticket_complexity_judgment
per_column.rationale: Intrinsic complexity drives both which ticket type/workload a ticket represents and how long it takes to resolve. A common cause not named in the query. (Arguably borderline with mediator, but as a pre-treatment intrinsic property it functions as a confounder.)

judge.rationale: The added set correctly instantiates a what-if intervention. ticket_type_primary is a genuine intervenable treatment: it is the settable lever named in the query (ticket types whose workload could be 'reduced'), and it is manipulable via routing/policy rather than being an immutable attribute. Three additional columns serve as plausible confounders -- common causes of both ticket type/workload and resolution time -- none of which are named in the query, which is exactly the capability under test. Agent assignment and ticket scope are solid confounders; complexity is somewhat borderline (could be read as a mediator of workload) but is best treated as a pre-treatment intrinsic driver. Overall this satisfies both parts of the technical claim: an intervenable treatment plus non-trivial, query-external confounders adjusted for before reading off the counterfactual effect.
